details:
**Plucked chicken: "Behold, a man!"**
When Plato defined man as a "featherless biped," Diogenes plucked a chicken, brought it to the Academy, and declared "Behold! I've brought you a man!" According to the story, Plato then added "with broad, flat nails" to his definition. This is the most common clue for Diogenes.

**Lamp in search of an "honest man"**
Diogenes famously wandered around in broad daylight carrying a lit lamp or lantern, claiming he was searching for an honest man. The stunt mocked the vice and deceit he saw in the society around him.

**Alexander the Great: "Stand out of my light"**
When Alexander the Great visited Diogenes and offered him anything he wished, Diogenes asked only that Alexander step aside because he was blocking the sunlight. Alexander supposedly replied, "If I were not Alexander, I would wish to be Diogenes."

**Founder of Cynicism ("the dog")**
Diogenes is regarded as the founder, or the most famous early figure, of the Cynic school. Critics called him a "dog" for his shameless public behavior, and the school's name comes from the Greek word kynikos, meaning "dog-like."

**Living in a pithos (tub or barrel)**
Diogenes lived in a large ceramic storage jar called a pithos, often described as a tub or barrel, in the marketplace (agora) of Athens. It is the best-known example of his deliberate poverty.

**Student of Antisthenes**
Diogenes was a follower of Antisthenes, a pupil of Socrates who is often seen as the forerunner of Cynicism. In one story, Antisthenes tried to drive Diogenes away by beating him with a staff, but Diogenes refused to leave and became his disciple.

**Diogenes Laertius, Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers**
A later writer who shares the name Diogenes, nicknamed Laertius, wrote this biographical compilation, probably in the 3rd century AD. It is a principal source for ancient Greek philosophy, and many of the anecdotes about Diogenes of Sinope come from it.

**"Deface the currency"**
According to one story, the Oracle of Delphi told Diogenes to "deface the currency." This was linked to an episode in Sinope in which Diogenes, or his father, a moneyer, debased the city's coinage, leading to his exile. Diogenes took the phrase as a motto for overturning conventional values.

**Sold into slavery: "ruling men"**
After being captured by pirates and put up for sale as a slave, Diogenes said that the only thing he was good at was "ruling men." He pointed to a buyer, traditionally the Corinthian Xeniades, and said that this man needed a master.

**Shamelessness, self-sufficiency, and asceticism**
Diogenes' philosophy rested on self-sufficiency (autarkeia), shamelessness, outspokenness (parrhesia), and a simple life lived "according to nature." He openly rejected social convention, for example by eating, urinating, and defecating in public.

**Spitting in a rich man's face**
While at a wealthy man's house, Diogenes was told not to spit because everything was so clean. He spat in the host's face, saying it was the only dirty place he could find.

**Refuting Eubulides' "horned" paradox**
Eubulides of Megara posed a sophism: "What you have not lost, you still have; you have not lost horns, so you have horns." Diogenes is said to have refuted it simply by touching his forehead.

**Diogenes of Apollonia**
A Presocratic philosopher with the same name who held that air is the fundamental substance. He is credited with suggesting that meteorites come from outer space, and Aristotle preserved his description of the blood vessels.

**Diogenes of Oenoanda**
An Epicurean of the 2nd century AD who had Epicurus's teachings carved into an enormous inscription on a portico wall in his hometown of Oenoanda in Lycia, in modern Turkey.
